>

  academics waiting in the wings to assume their publishing and/or
  teaching positions?  How does losing one's job prevent one from
  seeking (or finding) truth?  And is that distinct from The Truth?

    Regarding Christopher Brand:  this guy was mixing up race theory
  with pedophila as if there is some connection that we're missing.
  They might independently each qualify for scholarly inquiry, however
  I would imagine that combination of the two was understandably being
  received as inappropriate, running along just a wee bit too far down
  that garden path of seduction for pedagogical tastes.  TK had already
  anticipated such developments as pathological trends inherent to the
  "industrial-technological system" with:

   ._______________________________________________________________.
   |                                                               |
   |     "Propaganda for example is used for many good purposes,   |
   |      such as discouraging child abuse or race hatred. [14]"   |
   |_______________________________________________________________|


  and we may note TK's juxtaposition of "abuse" with "hatred" in the
  two overlapping incongruous contexts which nailed Christopher Brand.

    Now Ms. Gottfredson was offered $177,541 by the Pioneer Fund to
  conduct research (www.s-light.demon.co.uk/stories/genewar06.htm, or
  www.ferris.edu/ISAR/Institut/pioneer/search.htm). When her University
  (who is the employer) intervened to say she could not accept those
  moneys on the grounds of something similar to an academic "conflict of
  interest" then Ms. Gottfredson was faced with a -choice- to continue
  teaching or to resign and run with the Pioneer Fund.  Nobody doubts
  that $177,541 would have been the bottom of the barrel for her, nor
  that she might have sought employment at another University where she
  could also accept Pioneer Funds.  The crux of this issue centers on
  whether Universities can rightfully exert controls over their faculty
  by conditioning employment according to standards they are free to
  develop internally.  Of course, with regards to the Law and Higher
  Education, appeals processes remain available for those who wish to
  take it to the courts, yet I couldn't locate any litigation which may
  have documented that eventuality.  I agree that any case-law in that
  area might be of interest.  A University does not expect professorial
  staff energies to be diverted away from obligations at teaching and
  core-curricular refinement.  Furthermore the University is sometimes
  itself in a precarious funding position and is by no means completely
  independent of its obligation to the surrounding business community
  or to taxpayers.  "Academic freedom" is a nice-sounding phrase, yet
  for all intents and purposes we might say that it is mythological in
  certain controversial areas, and isn't exempt from the drumbeat of
  those objectionably platitudinous charges.  The issues being worked
  aren't so much those establishing mensuration of "racial variation"
  in a rapidly-changing educational context and/or compositional mixing
  but what to do about social policy, given stipulation of parameters.


>> What novel conclusions had you expected Ms. Gottfredson to draw?
>
> It is conventionally -- and erroneously -- believed that social
> inequalities are necessarily the result of discrimination. Plenty of
> evidence points to significant differences among individuals, groups,
> and races as far as intelligence, specifically. Given the extent of
> diversity in our society, and the pervasive belief that there is some
> sort of bogey man holding certain groups down, and given that we have
> not conclusively proven to what _extent_ these differences might be
> due to genetics, I see plenty of justification for Ms. Gottfredson to
> continue her research into this area. I'm sure she covers many other
> other areas, but the unusual focus into this has been made not by
> her, but, paradoxically, by insecure PC'ers.

    The "conclusive proof" is available by creating opportunities and
  allowing them to succeed or to wash-out in higher-education courses.
  It seems to me, however, that once deciding opportunities should not
  be allowed (on pretext of "genetic" impairment applied to classes of
  individuals rather than to the individuals themselves) then one would
  effectively -sabotage- a viability of any further "conclusive proof"
  in the evaluative context of those higher-education courses.  Instead
  our anticipated consequences of what Ms. Gottfredson's "research" is
  going to accomplish would seem to be that of denying actual "research"
  in those classroom settings which were designed to provide preparatory
  assessments for candidacy with professions in the real world.  The
  notion of pre-judging individuals based on "genetic" profiling might
  have been similar to the former Soviet Union's testing practices for
  pre-determining life stations, but is inconsistent with democratic
  principles in the free society based on individual rights.  Also, the
  denial of opportunities would instead perpetuate class hegemony and
  result in anti-competitive trade arrangements, impinging productivity.


> Yes, Ms. Gottfredson is very much a humanitarian. She and her
> daughters, who are twins by the way, are in the Peace Corps and
> assist impoverished people in the Third World. As far as you
> suggesting her work is unecessary and redundant, I think that is
> among the most idiotic things I have ever heard, literally.

   Twins strike me as redundant, however I'm not about to say that
  redundancy in one working aspect implies redundancy in other areas.
  Ms. Gottfredson wasn't being judged when the University informed her
  of policies, because their policies were developed for all faculty
  at that institution.  It's possible that her "research" would have
  later been found redundant, and also possible that she might come
  to acknowledgement -after- locating previously unknown studies that
  show strong isomorphism to a study she had recently completed.  No
  research project is exempt from the dustbin, and I think we're all
  on the same sheet of music when requesting research projects that
  may retain significant lasting value and not be outmoded in merely
  a few years by rapidly changing circumstances of a mobile society.
  Somebody else can utilize those Pioneer Funds and publish research
  even if Ms. Gottfredson isn't directly involved, or she can take
  some sabbatical / "leave of absense" during the interim, returning
  to university professorship after having completed her mission.
  These sorts of "conflict of interest" matters can occur frequently
  and may be resolved amicably, as "those who know" already know.


> ... there is a major difference between racism and discrimination
> -- although they are often confused, even by academics! I'm just
> pointing out that, in theory, racism is what drives racial
> discrimination and, by extension, the reputed glass ceiling.

  If "racism" is the cause of discrimination, then you're saying that
  were "racism" removed, we could mitigate/minimize discrimination?


> There are lots of _facts_ PC'ers are not willing to accept...
> Thankfully, the internet is an equalizer which is enabling more
> people to see the other side.

     Yes, and perhaps on the internet we may stipulate certain
   _facts_, however unacceptable they may seem, but then not fail
   to move along to a discussion of effective policy response.


> ... I don't recall saying a person has a "right" to hate
> someone who does him harm.  However, I may have said that along the
> way, and if I did, I certainly didn't mean it in a legal manner.  I
> meant if you care for a relative, and someone unjustifiably does harm

> I am atheist and a right-winger, but because I think God is a
> fairy-tale does not mean I look down on other right-wingers.

    How do you reconcile atheism (which denies God's existence) with
  the proposition "God is a fairy-tale" (since fairy-tales exist)?

    Double-negatives don't necessarily render a positive, and also
  one might dislike certain political groups because they are -not-
  sufficiently radical, or simply because they do not share common
  interests (i.e. were "hippie protestors" conversant in "boundary
  functions" and/or general mathematical topics?).  To illustrate
  my first point:  in mathematics we sometimes encounter the phrase
  "non-zero" which can be interpreted to mean "positive or negative"
  or it might mean an imaginary quantity, or it might not even be a
  number:  the word "cat" is also an example of "non-zero" if "cat"
  is not considered the same as the numeral or number zero.  When
  encountering political criticism, it would be erroneous to claim
  that "left criticism" implied an author's right-wing sympathy, or
  vice-versa.  In order to establish alliances one needs to locate
  positive evidence, since one can't prove a negative nor can one
  demonstrate a positive by a negative in context of open systems.

  The closest I can find, from the Manifesto, is TK's affiliation
  with anarchism, which is completely at variance to the corporate
  right-wing, or to platitudinous National Socialism, since TK used
  the phrase "our particular brand of anarchism" in footnote #34.
  Elsewhere TK is extraordinarily verbose on how both "right-wing"
  and "left-wing" desire High-Technology as a means of controlling
  their organizations and national electorate.  The bottom line is
  that TK cannot be categorized even remotely near the right-wing.
